svg.title: Security group tags: identity becomes a label, the label becomes a policy matrix, and the three ways to carry it across the network
svg.desc: Top: the flow. The endpoint authenticates, the policy server assigns a tag - employee ten, guest twenty, printer thirty, server forty - and the tag travels with the traffic either inline as a command field in the Ethernet frame, synchronised by SXP, or mapped statically by IP. The enforcement point - switch, firewall or fabric - looks up the source tag against the destination tag in one matrix and permits or denies. Middle left: a four by four matrix where employee to server is allowed on the application port, guest to everything except the internet is denied, printer to printer is allowed and printer to server is allowed only on the print protocol, and server to server is denied by default. Middle right: the three implementation methods and their limits. Inline tagging needs hardware support and the tag is lost across a Layer 3 boundary. SXP synchronises IP to tag mappings but has a learning delay and breaks when DHCP reassigns an address. Static mapping is simple and needs maintenance whenever an address changes. Bottom: the layered relationship - 802.1X confirms identity, SGT grants permission, the firewall and IPS inspect content, and micro-segmentation prevents lateral movement - with a warning that SGT performs authorisation only and no inspection, so a compromised endpoint wearing an employee tag still reaches everything an employee may reach.
svg.text: SGT: stop writing policies about addresses, write them about identity
An address changes when the user moves; a tag does not. The whole benefit and the whole cost come from that one substitution
THE FLOW · AUTHENTICATE, TAG, CARRY, ENFORCE
The tag is a 16-bit value carried inside the Ethernet frame. Because it is Layer 2 metadata, it is
preserved across a switch and lost across a router - which is exactly why SXP and static mapping exist.
ONE MATRIX, NOT N ACLS PER DEVICE
Four tags give sixteen decisions in one place, and the file survives every re-addressing project.
THREE WAYS TO CARRY THE TAG
Coverage: the Layer 2 domain. Needs hardware on every hop, and the tag dies at the router.
Coverage: across devices without inline support. Learning delay, and DHCP reuse of an
Coverage: servers and fixed devices. Free to start, and a maintenance cost at every
The practical stack is all three: inline in the campus, SXP where the hardware is old, static for servers.
"SGT REPLACES THE FIREWALL" - THE USUAL MISTAKE
SGT authorises (may this tag reach that tag). It does not inspect.
A compromised endpoint wearing the employee tag still reaches everything an
employee may reach - the matrix happily permits the attack.
Authorisation without inspection is half a control.
802.1X → who you are · SGT → where you may go
Firewall / IPS → what you bring in · micro-segmentation → where you spread
No layer replaces another; compressing all four into "we deployed SGT"
means authorisation was done and inspection was skipped
Orchestration test: adding one application should mean one matrix edit. If it still means ACLs on nine devices, the tag layer was bought but not adopted.
